text: Welcome to the clinic. Also, has there been any recent exposure to infections or complications during birth?

speaker: Patient
text: Newborn, born after the 32nd gestational week. The baby was born via cesarean delivery. The mother had gestational diabetes but was otherwise healthy with no other pregnancy-related diseases.

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for that background. Given the preterm birth and C-section, have you noticed if the baby is gasping or making grunting noises? Has the baby been able to feed normally, or are they stopping to breathe? REQUEST TEST: Pulse_Oximetry

speaker: Doctor
text: The oxygen saturation is 88%, which indicates hypoxemia. Are you observing any specific chest retractions, nasal flaring, or the "grunting" sound I asked about earlier? REQUEST TEST: Arterial_Blood_Gas; REQUEST IMAGES: Chest_X-Ray

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Arterial_Blood_Gas: pH 7.30 (slightly acidic), PaCO2 50 mm Hg (elevated), PaO2 60 mm Hg (reduced), HCO3- 24 mEq/L, Base_Excess -5. Chest_X-Ray: Ground-glass appearance, air bronchograms, suggesting Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS).

speaker: Doctor
text: The arterial blood gas indicates respiratory acidosis, and the chest X-ray confirms ground-glass opacities with air bronchograms, which is classic for Respiratory Distress Syndrome in a preterm infant. Is the baby currently responding to the oxygen therapy, and have you noticed any signs of surfactant deficiency such as worsening distress after birth?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Respiratory distress. I also have Tachypnea, Subcostal and intercostal retractions, Nasal flaring, Cyanosis.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS) in a preterm infant. The combination of prematurity (32 weeks), classic physical signs (retractions, flaring, cyanosis), hypoxemia, respiratory acidosis, and chest X-ray findings of ground-glass opacities with air bronchograms confirms the diagnosis of surfactant deficiency.
